The Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia has been red-flagged after several cars suffered power unit gremlins during a wet set of formation laps.

After a heavy tropical thunderstorm, the action at Malaysian Sepang was set to get underway with a number of laps behind the safety car followed by a standing start.

But ahead of F1's first-ever wet event under the 2026 regulations, a number of cars suffered power unit gremlins in the rain, suspected to be software-related.

Initially, polesitter Max Verstappen reported a lack of acceleration from his Red Bull before the Dutchman got going again. Soon after, second-placed Lewis Hamilton reported a similar issue on his Ferrari, with the Briton crawling around the first formation lap as the rest of the field passed him. One lap later, Hamilton too managed to get going again.

More cars, including Racing Bulls man Liam Lawson, Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto and Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas, also appeared to struggle with similar problems, with race control suspending the start procedure and throwing a red flag.

With the grid mixed up as cars streamed into pitlane, race control will revert to the original grid positions when the running is resumed.

Max Verstappen led the pack behind the initial safety car. Alex Bierens de Haan/LAT Images

A deluge of rain as the cars arrived on the grid resulted in the start of the race being delayed by 40 minutes before the first attempt was made to get racing underway behind a safety car.

But before the cars could complete a single lap behind the safety car, a bug in the software supplied to all teams by the FIA resulted in multiple drivers losing power and dropping down the order.

The resulting delay meant the start of the race was over 90 minutes behind schedule.

"When there is some kind of error or glitch, or whatever you want to call it, that's the problem.

Once racing got underway, the track dried up and the grand prix featured two further safety car periods to clear cars that retired from the race in dangerous locations.

[George Russell](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5503), who retired with a power unit issue under the final safety car period, said the fans that turned up to Malaysia's first grand prix since 2017 deserved a better show.

"The whole day felt like a bit of a faff, with the delay and then the red flag and then endless laps under the safety car and then suddenly doing extra laps to allow [Sergio Pérez] to overtake [behind the safety car], it didn't feel very F1 today," he said.

Open Extended Reactions

"Horrible," "sad," and "totally unacceptable" were among the reactions of Formula 1's drivers to the sport's attempt at racing in wet conditions at Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

A deluge of rain as the cars arrived on the grid resulted in the start of the race being delayed by 40 minutes before the first attempt was made to get racing underway behind a safety car.

But before the cars could complete a single lap behind the safety car, a bug in the software supplied to all teams by the FIA resulted in multiple drivers losing power and dropping down the order.

Initially [Max Verstappen](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4665), who was set to start from pole position, lost power, before [Lewis Hamilton](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=868), who was alongside him on the front row of the grid, ground to a halt and had to restart his Ferrari's power unit on the pit straight.

The FIA later said that "an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars."

But several drivers chose to sum up the situation more concisely, pointing the finger squarely at this year's complicated power unit regulations.

"\[It was\] horrible," reigning champion [Lando Norris](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5579) said. "It proves that we shouldn't have any of that stuff on the electronic side."

When the issue became apparent, all cars were told to return to the pits, where a software patch was supplied by the FIA and uploaded by each team.

The resulting delay meant the start of the race was over 90 minutes behind schedule.

"We missed some good racing, wet tires at the beginning, we should have been out there running," Aston Martin driver [Lance Stroll](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4775) said. "Instead cars are fixing their software issues. It's a bit sad to see."

Cadillac driver [Sergio Pérez](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4472) added: "I mean, it's obviously not great what happened today -- I'm sure we will learn from it as a sport, but what happened today is totally unacceptable for the sport."

\- **[Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires](https://www.espn.com/f1/story/_/id/50074959/max-verstappen-wins-pole-kimi-antonelli-extends-title-lead-sepang-formula-1-bahrain-gp-malaysia)**

\- **[Bahrain GP in Malaysia: George Russell suffers major title blow after race retirement](https://www.espn.com/f1/story/_/id/50074961/bahrain-gp-george-russell-malaysia-sepang-formula-1)**

\- **[George Russell on Bahrain GP retirement: 'Beyond disappointment' as title chances all but over](https://www.espn.com/f1/story/_/id/50074962/george-russell-bahrain-gp-retirement-disappointment-title-chances-all-sepang-formula-1)**

For many drivers, it was further proof that this year's regulations, which were designed so that nearly 50% of the car's power comes from its battery, are overcomplicated.

"That's the problem that we have, these engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented," race winner Verstappen said. "When there is some kind of error or glitch, or whatever you want to call it, that's the problem.

"I triggered it first, then I look in my mirror, and I just see everyone ... I was like, wait, are they waiting for me or?"

Hamilton, who finished third, likened the situation to Lego's marketing stunt at the British Grand Prix, where all the drivers were given electric go-karts to race against each other.

"It was like the Lego race!" Hamilton said while sitting next to Verstappen at the postrace news conference.

"Yeah, we had the same speed," Verstappen responded.

[Kimi Antonelli](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5829), who finished second in Sunday's race, chimed in: "It was insane. Like at some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn't understand what was going on."

Williams driver [Carlos Sainz](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4686) called on the sport to "have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation."

"It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the \[power units\], for the manufacturers. It is too complicated," he said. "Again, my only question mark is who, five years ago, decided that this was the direction to go? We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided four or five years ago, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago is wrong. ...

"Not a lot more to say -- just learn as a sport not to do those mistakes again and not suffer from the same strange cases."

Once racing got underway, the track dried up and the grand prix featured two further safety car periods to clear cars that retired from the race in dangerous locations.

[George Russell](https://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5503), who retired with a power unit issue under the final safety car period, said the fans that turned up to Malaysia's first grand prix since 2017 deserved a better show.

"The whole day felt like a bit of a faff, with the delay and then the red flag and then endless laps under the safety car and then suddenly doing extra laps to allow \[Sergio Pérez\] to overtake \[behind the safety car\], it didn't feel very F1 today," he said.

"I'd have been a bit disappointed if I was in the stands, watching that unfold, so ... that wasn't good."

Mark Schofield

Sun, October 4, 2026 at 2:32 PM UTC

Formula 1's return to the Sepang International Circuit for the first time since 2017 was a memorable one for Max Verstappen. Not only had Verstappen won that final Malaysian Grand Prix back in 2017, but this weekend he secured pole position for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia — his first pole position in nearly a calendar year — but he picked up his first win of the season by taking the checkered flag.

But the main story might just be what did, and did not, happen when the lights went out at the start of the race.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Advertisement

Between downpours, and a "software issue," the start of the race was delayed twice, first for 40 minutes due to the rain, and then for another 33 minutes after a failed start in the wet conditions.

When F1 tried to start the race after the initial 40-minute delay, race stewards called for at least two exploratory formation laps, hoping to get the race underway as conditions improved. But during that first speed-controlled lap, Verstappen reported over the radio that his Red Bull was struggling to accelerate.

Lewis Hamilton, set to start second, reported even more problems, which sent him down the pecking order on the grid. Hamilton eventually came to a halt on pit lane while Haas and Cadillac cars — also using Ferrari power units — came to stops at various points on the track.

That led to the second delay, as the cars were restored to their original positions on the grid, and the teams worked through various software updates to rectify the loss of power. The starting procedure was again suspended:

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord explained the issue to _Sky Sports F1_ during the second delay. "All the teams have been sent some new parameters to load into the cars as well which is happening up and down the grid," [said](https://www.skysports.com/f1/news/13594860/bahrain-gp-in-malaysia-max-verstappen-wins-first-race-of-2026-f1-season-in-wild-rain-hit-grand-prix-as-lewis-hamilton-surges-back) Lord. "There may have been something, a sort of software issue of some kind that was behind some of the difficulties we saw earlier."

Advertisement

Advertisement

Advertisement

Eventually, the race began, and Verstappen secured his first win of the season ahead of Antonelli and Hamilton. But the pre-race chaos was the major talking point after the checkered flag.

"You know, these engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented. And, yeah, when there's like some kind of… I want to call it… That's the problem. And, yeah, I triggered it first and then I look in my mirror, I just see… I was like, "Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going…?" It was like the Lego race," described Verstappen in the FIA Press Conference, referencing the LEGO Drivers' Parades that F1 has implemented ahead of a few races.

That was ahead of this sequence from Verstappen and Hamilton:

> **Hamilton:**"Well, I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."
>
> **Verstappen:** "Yeah, what can you say? I mean, that's not what you want, right, for the sport."
>
> **Hamilton:**"Yeah, I hope there is a lesson learned."
>
> **Hamilton: "** No, but it was because they had to update the software and then you have to load it into the car. I guess some had some faster laptops than others," said Hamilton when asked about the delay.
>
> **Verstappen: "** Yeah, that was the delay, just getting the software transferred, I guess, for everyone.

Many drivers questioned the decision to allows the cars that had stopped the chance to start the race, including Fernando Alonso. "It's the first time I see it," he [said](https://www.racefans.net/2026/10/04/fia-blames-unprecedented-circumstances-for-car-stoppages-on-formation-lap/). "I had half of the races this year with DNF and we never stopped the race. I hope they can do it next time we stop."

Advertisement

Advertisement

Advertisement

Following the race the FIA, F1's governing body, issued a statement promising a "full review" of the issue, and highlighting an "unprecedented combination" of factors at the start of the race:

"On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars," began the statement.

"As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race.

Advertisement

Advertisement

"This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue."

With his second-place finish, and a retirement from teammate George Russell, Antonelli moved a step closer to securing his first F1 Drivers' Championship. The young Mercedes driver now has an 84-point lead over Russell, as the season enters its closing stretch.

F1 returns to action next weekend with the Singapore Grand Prix.

[Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One "Formula One"), abbreviated to F1, is the highest class of [open-wheeled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-wheel_car "Open-wheel car") [auto racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto_racing "Auto racing") defined by the [Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Internationale_de_l'Automobile "Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile") (FIA), motorsport's world governing body.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-1) The "formula" in the name refers to a set of rules to which all participants and vehicles must conform.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-2) The Formula One World Championship season consists of a series of races, known as [Grands Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Formula_One_Grands_Prix "List of Formula One Grands Prix"), usually held on purpose-built [circuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Formula_One_circuits "List of Formula One circuits"), and in a few cases on [closed city streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_circuit "Street circuit").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-3) The results of each race are combined to determine two annual championships, [one for drivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Formula_One_World_Drivers'_Champions "List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions") and [one for constructors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Formula_One_World_Constructors'_Champions "List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-4) A [red flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_flags#Red_flag "Racing flags") is shown when there has been a crash or the track conditions are poor enough to warrant the race being stopped. The flags are displayed by the [marshals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorsport_marshal "Motorsport marshal") at various points around the circuit.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-5) A [Global Positioning System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System "Global Positioning System") (GPS) marshalling system was introduced in 2007. It involves a display of flag signals in the driver's cockpit, which alerts them to the crash.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-6) Following a red flag being shown, the exit of the [pit lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pit_stop "Pit stop") is closed and cars must proceed to the pit lane slowly without overtaking, lining up at the pit exit.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-Suspend-7) From 2005, a ten-minute warning is given before the race is resumed behind the [safety car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_car "Safety car"), which leads the field for a lap before it returns to the pit lane.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-8) Previously, the race was restarted in race order from the penultimate lap before the red flag was shown.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-9) If a race is unable to be resumed, "the results will be taken at the end of the penultimate lap before the lap during which the signal to suspend the race was given".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-Suspend-7) If 75% of the race distance has not been completed and the race cannot be resumed, half points are awarded. Until [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Formula_One_World_Championship "2015 Formula One World Championship"), no points were supposed to be awarded if the race could not be restarted and less than two laps had been completed,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-points-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-11) but starting in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Formula_One_World_Championship "2016 Formula One World Championship") this rule was updated to "no points if two laps or less have been completed".[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_red-flagged_Formula_One_races#cite_note-12) Since [the first World Championship Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_British_Grand_Prix "1950 British Grand Prix") in 1950, red flags have been shown in 91 World Championship Formula One races, with the latest one being at the [2026 Italian Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Italian_Grand_Prix "2026 Italian Grand Prix"). The FIA revealed an “unprecedented” glitch caused several cars to stop in the chaotic start to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Heavy rain in Sepang caused a delayed start but when the drivers left the pit lane, multiple drivers almost grinded to a halt including race leader Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton with several drivers in the midfield also experiencing issues.

The start procedure was abandoned and the Grand Prix eventually started properly with the original grid order almost an hour after the carnage.

"On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars," said the FIA in a statement.

"As a result, the FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the Power Unit before the start of the race.

"This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and Power Unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue."

"Basically, if you run the engines too slowly, the turbo spools down because we don't have the MGU-H anymore," he said.

"What's effectively happening is if you are off throttle for too long, the turbo spools down and when the drivers puts their foot back down it uses all the engine juice.

"As soon as the battery goes flat, you are down to internal combustion engine power only. And because it can't reach the drivers' torque demand anymore, because the engine is not creating the power because you have no turbo, you go outside of the FIA regulation.

### 'Not good enough' - Drivers react to bizarre scenes

Most drivers were unimpressed by the scenes and the extra hour's delay it took for the FIA to implement new software into the cars before the proper race start.

"At first, I thought that the Safety Car had switched off the light," said Ferrari's Charles Leclerc who was running fourth on the first formation lap.

"I couldn't see the Safety Car. There too much spray and I thought the Safety Car had gone, and Max was taking the gap to warm up the tyres.

"Then they told me on radio, 'we think Max has a problem', then Max went then Lewis was slow. I waited then at one point was like, 'okay I'm going to go' then when I went on the throttle, I had exactly the same problem and I realised everyone was in the same boat and we were stuck at 20kph.
